walkthroughs.body_html:
Changing Spaces; Making Places — a core area of A-Level Geography.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Changing Spaces; Making Places brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Changing Spaces; Making Places.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: What is the sequence of headland erosion from crack to stump?
options: Stacks form when the sea level rises and floods a hill.
Crack to cave to arch to stack to stump — waves widen cracks into caves, two caves meet to form an arch, the arch collapses leaving a stack, and the stack erodes to a stump.
Stacks form where rocks fall from the cliff into the sea.
Managed retreat means letting all coastal towns disappear into the sea.

mcqs.q: Why might managed retreat be more sustainable than building a sea wall?
options: Managed retreat means letting all coastal towns disappear into the sea.
Sea walls always solve coastal erosion problems permanently.
Sea walls are expensive, deflect erosion elsewhere and reflect wave energy worsening beach loss; managed retreat works with natural processes, creates habitat and is cheaper long-term.
Stacks form when the sea level rises and floods a hill.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between primary and secondary effects of an earthquake?
options: Stacks form when the sea level rises and floods a hill.
Primary effects happen first and secondary effects happen the next day.
Primary effects are the worst effects and secondary effects are minor.
Primary effects occur immediately as a direct result of shaking (building collapse, deaths); secondary effects follow afterwards (fires, tsunamis, disease, homelessness).
